title: They're people
hook: "they're slaves" "no, they're people, they're housemates, humble friends" (Letters 47)

segments.voice: Yesterday: lucus. Your line was the grove. Did you find an old tree, and a steady person who stirred the same awe? Day four hundred sixty-two.

A Roman dinner party. The master reclines and eats more than he can hold. Around the couches, enslaved people stand all night, silent and hungry. One clears up what the drunken guests have spilled. One carves. One pours the wine. If any of them so much as coughs or hiccups, Seneca says, there's a beating. A few days ago we promised to look straight at this, and the forty-seventh letter is where Seneca himself does. It opens with a little argument, played out as if someone kept interrupting him. Today, the last day of this week in the letters: they're people.
screen: `A ROMAN DINNER, SERVED IN SILENCE.` → `A COUGH MEANS A BEATING.` → `SENECA LOOKS STRAIGHT AT IT.`

segments.voice: First, the argument. Someone says: they're slaves. Seneca answers: no, they're people. Slaves! No, housemates. Slaves! No, humble friends. Slaves! No, fellow slaves, if you remember that fortune has the same power over all of us. Four replies, each one closing the distance. Second, the same seeds. The one you call a slave, he says, was born of the same seeds, enjoys the same sky, breathes, lives and dies as you do. You could see him free; he could see you enslaved. Third, the proverb. Romans said: so many slaves, so many enemies. Seneca's answer: we don't have them as enemies; we make them so, by cruelty. Fourth, the honest part. Seneca never called for slavery to end. He owned many enslaved people himself, and his great household ran on their labor. His letter asks masters to be humane, to eat with those they trust, to talk with them. It doesn't ask them to let go. Both things are true: this letter is often counted among the most humane Roman writings on slavery, and it stops far short of freedom. Looking back on our week, from the rich man's library to the god within, this is where Seneca's large ideas meet a real dinner table. The divine in every mind has to include the person pouring the wine.
screen: `SLAVES! NO, PEOPLE.` · `BORN OF THE SAME SEEDS.` · `WE MAKE THEM ENEMIES.` · `HUMANE, BUT NOT FREEDOM.` · then, large: `THEY'RE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who served you this past week whose names you may not know: a cashier, a driver, a cleaner, someone on a support line, someone who cooked your food. Picture one face as clearly as you can. Same sky, same breath, same short life. Let that be true for a moment. If you know their name, say it silently. If you don't, notice that, without blame. The bell holds the time.
They're people. Seneca's forty-seventh letter answers 'slaves' four times: people, housemates, humble friends, fellow slaves. Humane, and still short of freedom. Today's word.

Your line: born of the same seeds. Thank someone who serves you today, by name if you can, and look them in the eye when you do. That's our week in the letters. Next week, more Seneca. Day four hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Many people who read this letter make a habit of learning and using the names of those who serve them, and of thanking them directly.

fork.setup: you're at a Roman dinner. a guest says, of the silent servers, 'they're slaves.' what does Seneca reply first?
fork.reveal: Seneca answers four times: people, housemates, humble friends, fellow slaves under the same fortune.

original.note: Latin, Seneca, Letters 47.1: they're slaves. No, they're human beings.

trapdoor: what you thought: Seneca was an ancient abolitionist.
what it means: he insisted enslaved people were fully human and should be treated humanely, without calling for their freedom.
what a scholar hears: Letters 47.1, 47.5, 47.10; contubernales, 'tent-mates' or housemates, is a military word; Seneca's own household was large, and Tacitus records that wealth.
recall: stern, refused to bend to Caesar

notes: Letters 47.1 ('Servi sunt.' 'Immo homines.' 'Servi sunt.' 'Immo contubernales.' 'Servi sunt.' 'Immo humiles amici.' 'Servi sunt.' 'Immo conservi'), 47.2–3 the dinner scene and punishment for a cough or hiccup, 47.5 the proverb 'quot servi, tot hostes', 47.10 same seeds. Gummere's wording deliberately not quoted (paraphrased). Confirm.

Seneca's ownership of many enslaved people and his wealth: widely accepted (Tacitus, Annals 13.42; 15.45, 15.64). Script now says only that 'his great household ran on their labor'; the stronger claim that his wealth rested on their labor was dropped as not clearly sourced.
'One of the most humane things written about slavery in Rome': a scholarly commonplace, but a judgment; soften if a Keeper prefers.
